text: Finding the root cause, which the last three lessons built a real method for, is only half of a live incident. The other half is a decision that has nothing to do with diagnosis: given what you now know, do you roll back the change that caused this, or fix the actual problem in place while the system stays as it is? Picking the wrong one under pressure costs real time and real risk.

Rolling back means reverting to the last known-good state. It's usually fast, often a single command or pipeline re-run, and it returns the system to something already verified. But it returns you to before, not fixed — the stale rule or missing permission is still there, waiting to resurface the next time someone makes a similar change.

Fixing forward means leaving the current state in place and applying the specific fix directly, resolving the root cause the first time. The real cost is time, since you have to diagnose fully and apply the fix correctly, and risk, since any change made mid-incident, under pressure, can introduce a second problem on top of the first.

The decision comes down to stakes and certainty, not a fixed rule. Lean toward rollback when the fix isn't fully tested yet or a large part of a production system is down. Lean toward fixing forward when the root cause and the fix are both small and clearly identified, with a limited blast radius — one rule, one role, one resource.

Lesson 32's NSG fix is the second case: a one-line source IP correction on an existing rule, small and well understood enough that fixing forward made more sense than rolling back an entire deployment. An unfamiliar production change with half the system degraded is the opposite case. Neither approach is automatically the professional one — reading the specific situation is the actual skill, and it's exactly what the capstone starting in Chapter 8 will ask you to do on a full build.
